- If sentiment history shows any positive values (especially 0.33 or 0.25), model should not assume continuation of prior trend; instead, adjust downward with increasing urgency as sentiment rises.
- Model consistently overestimates early in forecast horizon (first 5–10 days) — apply downward bias of 1–3% for first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- After a spike in price (e.g., >75), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply “lag correction”: if true outcome drops after spike, reduce forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 days.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 78→70→68→65), model should not assume continuation — apply “reversion buffer”: forecast should be capped at 10–15% below recent peak if sentiment is flat or negative.
- When sentiment history is all 0.00, model should not assume trend continuation — treat as “neutral zone” and apply conservative, flat or slightly downward drift (0.5–1.5% per day) unless new sentiment emerges.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows sharp drop (e.g., 75→70→65), apply “sudden drop correction”: reduce forecast by 3–5% for next 3 days, then adjust to true trend if sentiment shifts.
- Sentiment spikes (0.33) correlate with true price drops — model should not overreact to sentiment; if sentiment rises, forecast should be adjusted downward by 1–2% per day for 3–5 days.
